summary: Describes 464XLAT, an architecture giving limited IPv4 connectivity across an IPv6-only network by combining stateless translation at the edge, as in RFC 6145, with stateful translation in the core, as in RFC 6146. It helps deploy IPv4 service quickly. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: 464XLAT lets an IPv4 application reach a global IPv4 server through an IPv6-only network. A translator at the customer edge and another at the provider edge convert the traffic between address formats.

questions: how do ipv4 apps work on ipv6 only networks
what is the difference between clat and plat
how does ipv4 traffic cross an ipv6 only network
subtitle: How IPv4 traffic can cross an IPv6-only network through two translators.

tldr.problem: An IPv6-only access network may still need to provide limited access to IPv4 servers for IPv4 applications.
tldr.mechanism: A customer-side CLAT performs stateless translation, and a provider-side PLAT performs stateful translation, carrying the traffic across the IPv6 network without encapsulation.
tldr.outcome: 464XLAT provides client-to-server IPv4 connectivity over IPv6-only networks but does not support inbound IPv4 connections or IPv4 peer-to-peer communication.

today: RFC 6877 is an Informational RFC published in April 2013. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Translation Approach
sections.content:
464XLAT combines stateless translation at the customer edge with stateful translation in the provider network. It reuses the translation methods described in RFC 6145 and RFC 6146 and does not require DNS64.

The architecture provides limited IPv4 service, not a full replacement for IPv4. The RFC limits it to the client-server model where the server has a global IPv4 address; it does not cover IPv4 peer-to-peer communication or inbound IPv4 connections.
sections.plainLanguage: An IPv4-only application can send traffic through an IPv6-only access network because translators change the packet addresses at each edge. The RFC limits this service to clients reaching IPv4 servers.

sections.title: The CLAT and PLAT Roles
sections.content:
The customer-side translator, or CLAT, follows the stateless translation method and maps private IPv4 addresses to IPv6 addresses and back. It can be implemented in a router or an end device. The provider-side translator, or PLAT, uses stateful translation between global IPv6 and global IPv4 addresses.

In a wireline network, IPv4 hosts behind the CLAT reach global IPv4 hosts through both translators, while IPv6 traffic can travel directly. In the wireless example, the user equipment provides a private IPv4 address and routes IPv4 traffic to the CLAT when an application needs IPv4.
sections.plainLanguage: The CLAT sits on the customer side and the PLAT sits in the provider network. IPv4 traffic crosses both, while IPv6-to-IPv6 traffic does not need translation.

sections.title: Addressing and Traffic Treatment
sections.content:
The CLAT needs IPv6 prefixes for its interfaces and for statelessly translated traffic, and it must discover the translation prefix used by the PLAT. If it cannot obtain a dedicated prefix for translation, it may use NAT44 for local IPv4 traffic before stateless translation.

The RFC’s traffic cases distinguish IPv6 applications reaching IPv6 servers, IPv6 applications reaching IPv4 servers, and IPv4 applications reaching IPv4 servers. These cases use no translation, stateful translation at the PLAT, or 464XLAT through both PLAT and CLAT, respectively.
sections.plainLanguage: The translation path depends on the address types used by the application and server. When both use IPv4, traffic passes through both translators; IPv6 traffic to an IPv6 server stays native.

sections.title: Implementation and Security Notes
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that a CLAT provide a DNS proxy and advertise itself as the DNS server for local clients. This lets ordinary DNS queries use native IPv6 across the access network; other DNS queries must still be allowed and translated like other traffic.

For security, the document directs PLAT implementations to the security considerations in RFC 6146 and CLAT implementations to those in RFC 6145. It also notes that a CLAT may follow RFC 6092.
sections.plainLanguage: A CLAT can proxy DNS so name lookups cross the access network as IPv6 traffic. The RFC points implementers to the security guidance for the underlying translation methods.
